sources.title: Southern multimammate mouse
sources.note: Cites Cassola F (2016), IUCN Least Concern.

summary: A small, terrestrial, nocturnal mouse of southern African grassland and semi-arid savannah, named for the eight to 12 pairs of mammae that run from the sternum to the inguinal region. It cannot be told from the Natal multimammate mouse by appearance alone; the two are separated by chromosome number and molecular markers. It is a habitat generalist and a prolific breeder, often abundant in disturbed or recovering ground, and has been recorded in Kruger National Park.
description: The 2016 EWT assessment, which treats this species together with the Natal multimammate mouse, gives the namesake mark as a large number of mammae, between eight and 12 pairs from the sternum to the inguinal region. It states that the two species are cryptic and cannot be distinguished by appearance, cranio-dental features, or a multivariate analysis, and are separated only by chromosome number (2n = 36 in M. coucha; 2n = 32 in M. natalensis) and molecular markers. Wikipedia agrees that they cannot be distinguished by superficial appearance, and adds that closer analysis has found anatomical differences in cranial, dental and phallic morphology, and physiological differences in haemoglobin pattern and pheromones. Coat colour, ear shape and other external marks were not described in the sources used. The sexes are not described as differently marked, apart from the mammae.
habits: Both species are described in the 2016 EWT assessment as terrestrial and nocturnal. M. coucha has a wide habitat tolerance in high-altitude, moderate-rainfall regions, is often associated with human-dominated landscapes, and is regularly found inside and around human dwellings. It is abundant in disturbed ground and in areas recovering from a natural disturbance, and may remain during and directly after a fire. It is a prolific, opportunistic breeder, and population eruptions often occur under favourable conditions. In Roan Camp, Kruger National Park, Kneidinger et al. (2014), as cited by EWT, found M. coucha in relatively more high-altitude, low-rainfall areas, whereas M. natalensis dominated in wetter areas. A more detailed Kruger-specific activity study was not found.

diet.summary: The 2016 EWT assessment, citing Monadjem et al. (2015), describes both Mastomys species as having a diet that varies from granivorous to omnivorous, sometimes including arthropods and carrion. Wikipedia describes M. coucha as an opportunist omnivore whose diet consists of a variety of plant and animal resources, including cannibalism when under severe resource limitation. A diet study confined to Kruger was not found. Diet details given by EWT for M. natalensis at Umvoti Vlei are not applied here.

young: The 2016 EWT assessment, citing Monadjem et al. (2015), says both M. coucha and M. natalensis are opportunistic breeders that can breed throughout the year when conditions are favourable, with breeding strongly correlated with rainfall; in most areas, however, reproduction does not occur during winter. They are prolific breeders and, although this rarely happens, can carry up to 24 foetuses at once under favourable conditions. Gestation and the interval between litters are relatively short, and litter size varies from 1 to 27 young. Kruger-specific birth months and a measured gestation length were not found.

predators.note: The 2016 EWT assessment says Mastomys species form a forage resource for carnivores, especially in post-fire landscapes, because they do not vacate an area after fire. It does not name a mammal species in this guide.

prey.note: The 2016 EWT assessment, citing Monadjem et al. (2015), says the diet of both Mastomys species sometimes includes arthropods.

habitat: The 2016 EWT assessment, citing Monadjem et al. (2015), restricts M. coucha to the grasslands and semi-arid savannahs of South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia, south of the Zambezi River, and describes a wide habitat tolerance in high-altitude, moderate-rainfall regions. It is often associated with human-dominated landscapes and is abundant in disturbed or recovering ground. Within South Africa it occurs widely in the central and northeastern interior, including Limpopo, Gauteng and most of Mpumalanga except the southern parts. Wikipedia adds open grassland, shrubland and semi-desert karoo, and lists Angola, Botswana, Lesotho, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa and Zimbabwe; EWT treats presence in Botswana, Mozambique and Swaziland as uncertain, and that disagreement is recorded rather than averaged. In Kruger National Park, Kneidinger et al. (2014), as cited by EWT, recorded the species in relatively more high-altitude, low-rainfall areas at Roan Camp.

size.note: One source claims a head-and-body length of 8.2–11.9 cm, a tail of 7–10.7 cm and a mass of 22–40 g (0.022–0.040 kg) for Mastomys coucha. Those figures are a published range for that species, not a combined Mastomys measurement and not a mean. A more accurate figure may be available at this URL: https://ewt.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/32.-Multimammate-Mouse-Mastomys-spp_LC.pdf

similar.note: The two species cannot be distinguished by appearance, cranio-dental features or a multivariate analysis. They are told apart by chromosome number (2n = 36 in M. coucha; 2n = 32 in M. natalensis) and by molecular markers. In South Africa they co-occur only marginally, with a possible zone of overlap along the eastern escarpment. In Kruger National Park both have been recorded at Roan Camp, where M. natalensis dominated wetter areas and M. coucha was found in relatively more high-altitude, low-rainfall areas (Kneidinger et al. 2014, as cited by the 2016 EWT assessment).

population.notes: No Kruger census or SANParks park-wide count was found. The 2016 regional assessment gives the regional population trend as stable or increasing and does not publish a Kruger total. It reports that, at Roan Camp, Kruger National Park, Mastomys spp. were the most abundant genus in, around and outside the enclosure, comprising 81% of captures (MacFadyen 2007); that figure is for the genus, not a park-wide count of M. coucha. A more accurate figure may be available at this URL: https://www.sanparks.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/KNP-wildlife-trends.pdf

research.note: This file follows species-list.json in treating the Kruger animal as Mastomys coucha (Multimammate mouse, the 2011 SANParks checklist name; Afrikaans Vaalveldmuis, as given in the 2016 EWT assessment). EWT 2016 and iNaturalist also list Southern Multimammate Mouse and Southern African Mastomys as English names. M. coucha and M. natalensis are cryptic and are told apart mainly by chromosomes (2n = 36 versus 2n = 32) and molecular markers; a separate file covers M. natalensis. The 2016 EWT assessment records both species in Kruger National Park at Roan Camp (Kneidinger et al. 2014), with habitat partitioning, so status is entered as resident rather than omitted. A 2025 EWT project page for this species was not found in the one site search; the 2025 fact sheet lists no status change, so conservation status follows the 2016 assessment (Least Concern; regional trend stable or increasing) and the IUCN global listing cited on Wikipedia. No published measurements and no licensable photograph suitable for display were found. A later search of iNaturalist place 113055 (southern Africa) returned only the same three licensed research-grade records already rejected, and a Wikimedia Commons search found no additional photograph with a southern African locality that was suitable for display.

gaps: No Kruger census or SANParks population figure was found. The 2016 regional assessment gives the regional trend as stable or increasing and does not publish a Kruger total. A report that Mastomys spp. made up 81% of captures at Roan Camp (MacFadyen 2007) is a genus-level local figure, not a park-wide count of M. coucha. A more accurate figure may be available at this URL: https://www.sanparks.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/KNP-wildlife-trends.pdf

No licensable photograph suitable for display was found. iNaturalist has 0 research-grade observations of Mastomys coucha in place 69020. A South Africa (place 6986) search returned three licensed research-grade records: one at Kathu was caught in a Sherman trap and photographed while handled; one at Nkangala (tagged Millstream) was taken against a building; and one from Gert Sibande District Municipality includes a ventral-up photograph of the mammae, so that animal was handled. M. coucha and M. natalensis cannot be distinguished by appearance, so photographs identified only to genus, or that could be either species, were not used.

A further iNaturalist search in southern Africa (place 113055) returned only those same three licensed research-grade records, already rejected as handled or taken against a building. A Wikimedia Commons search for Mastomys coucha found two CC BY-SA 3.0 photographs by Marcus33 with no locality, a copy of the already-rejected Gert Sibande photograph, and a parasitology PDF; none was suitable for display.
iNaturalist has 0 sound observations for Mastomys coucha in place 69020. No sourced description of the calls was found.

M. coucha and M. natalensis are cryptic sibling species, told apart mainly by chromosome number (2n = 36 versus 2n = 32) and molecular markers, not by appearance. This file follows species-list.json (Mastomys coucha) and does not attempt to re-identify Kruger records. The 2016 EWT assessment, citing Kneidinger et al. (2014), records both species at Roan Camp, Kruger National Park.

A 2025 EWT project page was not found in the one site search. The 2025 EWT Mammal Red List fact sheet does not list a status change for this species, so conservation status and much of the natural-history text follow the 2016 assessment.

Skinner and Chimimba and Stuart's field guide were not available as books. The 2016 EWT assessment and Wikipedia do not publish measurements, and Animal Diversity Web has only a classification page, so size is omitted.
Coat colour, ear colour and shape, eye colour, tail colour and shape, leg colour, a sexed size split and shoulder height were not given in the sources used, so those marks are null.

iNaturalist has 0 observations of any grade for this taxon in place 69020, although the species is on the 2011 SANParks checklist and the 2016 EWT assessment records it in Kruger. Kruger presence follows those sources.
No Kruger-specific breeding study or measured gestation length was found. Litter size and the figure of up to 24 foetuses are given by EWT for both Mastomys species together.
